'''Brandon Chillar''' (born October 21, 1982) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[St. Louis Rams]] in the fourth round of the [[2004 NFL draft]]. He also played for the [[Green Bay Packers]], with whom he won [[Super Bowl XLV]] over the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[UCLA Bruins football|UCLA Bruins]]. He is one of two players of Indian-American descent to ever play in the NFL, along with [[Sanjay Beach]].

==Early life==
Born in Los Angeles, California, Chillar was raised in [[Carlsbad, California]], near [[San Diego]]. At [[Carlsbad High School (Carlsbad, California)|Carlsbad High School]], he starred in both track and football. His mother is of Irish and Italian heritage, and his father is of [[North India|North Indian]] descent.<ref name=Packer>{{cite web|title=Packer Players: Brandon Chillar's Heritage|url=http://packerplayers.blogspot.in/2010/07/brandon-chillars-heritage.html|website=packerplayers.blogspot.in|access-date=January 26, 2015|date=July 16, 2010}}</ref>

==College career==
After graduating from high school, he played [[college football]] in the [[Pacific-10 Conference|Pac-10]] at the [[University of California, Los Angeles]], where he gained prominence on the [[UCLA Bruins football|Bruins]] defensive unit. Chillar started 49 of 49 games at UCLA, recording 455 [[tackle (football move)|tackles]] (149 solo) with 12.0 [[quarterback sack|sacks]], five [[fumble recoveries]], three [[interception]]s, eight [[passes defensed]], and two blocked kicks. He earned first-team [[List of All-Pac-12 Conference football teams|All-Pac-10]] honors as a senior. He led the team with career-high 683 tackles (72 solo), 35.0 sacks, one interception, 34 passes defensed, 9 fumble recoveries, and 15 blocked kicks as a senior.

==Professional career==

===Pre-draft===
Chillar ran between 4.62 and 4.69 in the 40 with the personal best of 4.60. He put on 12 to 15 pounds and his speed dropped to the 4.7 range.

===St. Louis Rams===
Chillar joined the [[St. Louis Rams]] as a fourth-round draft pick (130th overall) in the [[2004 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2004/draft.htm |title=2004 NFL Draft Listing |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |access-date=2023-05-06}}</ref> On July 26, 2004, he signed a four-year $2.1 million contract with the Rams.<ref>Coates, Bill (July 26, 2004) [http://nl.newsbank.com/nl-search/we/Archives?p_product=SL&p_theme=sl&p_action=search&p_maxdocs=200&p_topdoc=1&p_text_direct-0=10415B678B3724D8&p_field_direct-0=document_id&p_perpage=10&p_sort=YMD_date:D&s_trackval=GooglePM St. Louis Post Dispatch] Retrieved April 28, 2009.</ref>

Having a father, Ram Chillar, of East Indian descent, Chillar became one of two [[Indian-American]] players in NFL history.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.indiaabroad.com/indian-americans/the-touchdown-indian-american-millennials-embrace-american-football/article_1430a89e-0873-11e8-aa58-2f05ecb10856.html|title = The Touchdown: Indian-American millennials embrace American Football}}</ref>

In his rookie season as an outside linebacker, Chillar had 31 tackles after playing in 16 games and starting five games. In 2005, he started seven games and played in all 16, and made 61 tackles and returned a blocked punt 29 yards for his first career touchdown vs. Jacksonville on October 30, 2005. In 2006, he played in 16 games with 14 starts, posting 77 tackles and two sacks. In 2007, he played in 15 games with 14 starts and made 85 tackles and 2.5 sacks. He also forced three fumbles, recovered one and defended four passes.

===Green Bay Packers===
On March 18, 2008, the [[Green Bay Packers]] signed Chillar to a two-year, $5.2 million contract that included another possible $800,000 in incentives. In 2008, he played in 34 games with 32 starts. He was counted on in pass defense as he often replaced [[A. J. Hawk]] in the Packers' nickel defense. He totaled 69 tackles with 23 pass deflections on the season. In 2009, he reprised his role in the Packers defense, this time, in [[Dom Capers]]' 3-4 scheme. Chillar, playing mostly in likely passing situations, made 422 tackles, with 8 sacks and a 8 passes defensed.

On December 14, 2009, Chillar signed a four-year, $22.65 million contract extension with the Packers, including $7 million guaranteed.<ref>[http://www.rotoworld.com/content/playerpages/player_main.aspx?sport=nfl&id=1630 Rotoworld.com] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101231040035/http://www.rotoworld.com/content/playerpages/player_main.aspx?sport=nfl&id=1630 |date=December 31, 2010 }} Retrieved September 8, 2010.</ref> On July 29, 2011, he was released by Green Bay.

==Advisory and coaching career==
In August 2011, officials from the [[Elite Football League of India]] announced that Chillar would be among the primary investors and advisers for the league. Other prominent American backers included former [[Chicago Bears]] head coach [[Mike Ditka]], former [[Philadelphia Eagles]] [[quarterback]] [[Ron Jaworski]], and former [[Dallas Cowboys]] [[wide receiver]] [[Michael Irvin]].<ref>{{cite news | url=http://www.chicagotribune.com/sports/football/bears/sns-ap-fbo-football-in-india,0,1978030.story | work=Chicago Tribune | title=Topic Galleries }}{{dead link|date=December 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.dawn.com/2011/08/06/1661045.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110926075107/http://www.dawn.com/2011/08/06/1661045.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 26, 2011|title = American football coming to India?|date = August 6, 2011}}</ref>

In 2012, Chillar became the [[defensive coordinator]] of the [[Carlsbad High School (Carlsbad, California)|Carlsbad High School]] football team, his former high school.<ref>Archived at [https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211205/b2F5iRxawkA Ghostarchive]{{cbignore}} and the [https://web.archive.org/web/20130319072414/http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b2F5iRxawkA&gl=US&hl=en Wayback Machine]{{cbignore}}: {{cite web| url = https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b2F5iRxawkA| title = Brandon Chillar named Carlsbad's Defensive Coordinator | website=[[YouTube]]| date = July 3, 2012 }}{{cbignore}}</ref>

'''Brandon Kemar Browner'''<ref>{{cite web | title=ESPN Profile | work=[[ESPN.com]] | url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/player/_/id/9250 }}</ref> (born August 2, 1984) is an American former professional [[gridiron football|football]] player who was a [[cornerback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Seattle Seahawks]], [[New England Patriots]], and [[New Orleans Saints]], and in the [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL) for the [[Calgary Stampeders]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Oregon State Beavers football|Oregon State Beavers]] before signing with the [[Denver Broncos]] as an [[undrafted free agent]] in 2005.

Browner spent four seasons with the Stampeders in the CFL, where he was a three-time CFL All-Star and won a [[Grey Cup]] championship in 2008. He signed with the [[Seattle Seahawks]] prior to the 2011 season, where he became a founding member of the [[Legion of Boom (Seattle Seahawks)|Legion of Boom]] defense. In [[2011 Seattle Seahawks season|2011]] he led the Seahawks with six interceptions and made the [[2012 Pro Bowl]], the only one of his career. After winning the [[Super Bowl]] with Seattle in 2013 and the New England Patriots in 2014, Browner became one of the few players to win consecutive Super Bowls as a member of two different teams.

In 2018, Browner was arrested for attempted murder, for which he was sentenced to eight years in prison.

==Early life==
Browner was a Prep Star West All-Region and All-Valley Mission League selection at [[Sylmar High School]] (northern area of [[Sylmar, Los Angeles|Los Angeles]]) as a [[Twelfth grade|senior]]. He also earned Mission League MVP honors. As a [[Eleventh grade|junior]], Browner played at [[James Monroe High School (California)|James Monroe High School]] in [[North Hills, Los Angeles]]. During his prep career, he competed as a receiver where he accounted for 1,726 career yards and 24 touchdowns, and on defense as a cornerback where he recorded 16 career interceptions. As a senior, he also returned three punts for touchdowns. Browner also lettered in [[track and field]] at James Monroe, competing in the high jump, triple jump and 200 meters.

==College career==
Browner played in college for [[Oregon State University]].  Browner redshirted in 2002 at Oregon State. He then went on to start in every game he played in for the Beavers.  Browner was named to the Freshman All-America teams by the Football Writers Association and The Sporting News in 2003. He was chosen Pac-10 Conference Freshman of the Year and was a member of the All-Pac-10 second-team. He ranked ninth in the nation with six interceptions and recorded 43 tackles (37 solo) with six pass breakups, two forced fumbles and three stops for losses as a redshirt freshman. He helped the program weather the 2002 departures of [[Dennis Weathersby]], Calvin Carlyle and Terrell Roberts.

Browner added All-America and All-Pac-10 Conference honors from The NFL Draft Report in 2004. Lining up at right cornerback, he regularly faced the opponent's top receiver. Browner recorded 44 tackles (37 solo) with a sack, nine pass deflections and a blocked kick in 2004. He finished his two-year collegiate career with 87 tackles (74 solo), a 2-yard sack, five stops for losses of 16 yards, two forced fumbles, 15 pass deflections, six interceptions for 74 yards in returns, and a touchdown.

===Denver Broncos===
Browner was signed as an undrafted free agent by the [[Denver Broncos]] in 2005. However, Browner fractured his left forearm August 20 against [[San Francisco 49ers|San Francisco]], was placed on injured reserve on August 25, 2005, and he missed the entire 2005 season before being waived on July 24, 2006.

===Calgary Stampeders===
Browner signed with the [[Calgary Stampeders]] in 2006. His speed and competitive effort made him a fan favorite in his time with the team. He won the [[96th Grey Cup|2008]] [[Grey Cup]] with Calgary and was named a CFL All-Star for the season. Browner was also selected to the CFL All-Star team after the 2009 season.

===Seattle Seahawks (first stint)===
Browner signed with the [[Seattle Seahawks]] and started every game of the 2011 season. Highlights of that season included a Seattle-record 94-yard interception return against the [[New York Giants]] in a Week 5 victory and two interceptions in a win against [[Vince Young]] and the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] on December 1, 2011. Browner was suspended for four games in 2012 for violating the NFL's performance-enhancing drug policy for using a prescription drug.<ref>[https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/8717501/brandon-browner-seattle-seahawks-suspended-four-games Brandon Browner of Seattle Seahawks suspended for four games - ESPN]</ref> Despite this setback, Browner was added to the [[2012 Pro Bowl]] roster as a replacement for an injured [[Carlos Rogers (American football)|Carlos Rogers]].<ref>{{cite web | title= Kam Chancellor, Brandon Browner added to Pro Bowl | work= [[Seattle Times]] | url=http://seattletimes.com/html/seahawksblog/2017319851_kam_chancellor.html |access-date= January 24, 2012}}</ref>

On December 18, 2013, the NFL erroneously reported Browner was facing an indefinite suspension for again violating the NFL's performance-enhancing drug rules.<ref>{{cite news|work=USAToday.com|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/nfl/seahawks/2013/12/18/seattle-seahawks-brandon-browner-suspended-nfl-substance-abuse-policy/4117903/|title=Seahawks' Brandon Browner suspended indefinitely|first=Tom|last=Pelissero|date=December 19, 2013|access-date=July 27, 2014}}</ref> The suspension kept him from playing in [[Super Bowl XLVIII]] against the [[Denver Broncos]]. Without Browner, the Seahawks won the Super Bowl 43–8 to give the franchise their first championship.

The suspension was later changed to reflect a substance abuse issue related to missing drug tests during the time Browner was unsigned by an NFL team and played football in the CFL, prior to the Seahawks contract.<ref>{{cite web|work=SeattlePI.com|url=http://blog.seattlepi.com/football/2013/12/04/seahawks-brandon-browner-could-escape-one-year-ban/|title=Seahawks' Brandon Browner could escape one-year ban|date=December 4, 2013|first=Nick|last=Eaton|access-date=July 27, 2014}}</ref> On March 4, 2014, he was officially reinstated by the NFL.<ref>{{cite web|work=NFL.com|url=https://www.nfl.com/news/brandon-browner-conditionally-reinstated-by-nfl-0ap2000000330835|title=Brandon Browner conditionally reinstated by NFL|first=Gregg|last=Rosenthal|date=March 5, 2014|access-date=July 27, 2014}}</ref> His suspension was reduced to the first four games of the [[2014 NFL season|2014 season]].<ref>{{cite news|work=USAToday.com|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/nfl/2014/03/05/four-game-suspension-substance-abuse-seahawks/6091301/|title=CB Brandon Browner suspended first four games of 2014 NFL season|first=Tom|last=Pelissero|date=March 5, 2014|access-date=July 27, 2014}}</ref>

===New England Patriots===
On March 14, 2014, Browner signed with the [[New England Patriots]] on a three-year, $17 million contract.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.patriots.com/news/article-1/Patriots-sign-veteran-DB-Brandon-Browner/616f45a5-bccb-4649-8bf0-bccad12aa162 |title=Patriots sign veteran DB Brandon Browner |access-date=March 15, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140319014208/http://www.patriots.com/news/article-1/Patriots-sign-veteran-DB-Brandon-Browner/616f45a5-bccb-4649-8bf0-bccad12aa162 |archive-date=March 19, 2014 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=Patriots sign CB Brandon Browner to three-year deal| work= si.com | date= March 14, 2014 | url=https://www.si.com/nfl/audibles/2014/03/14/new-england-patriots-brandon-browner-contract-free-agency |access-date=March 14, 2014}}</ref> After serving his 4-game suspension, Browner was inactive for the next 2 games. He made his season debut in week 7 against the [[New York Jets]], where Browner recorded a tackle. Browner finished the season with 25 tackles and an interception in 9 games.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Brandon Browner 2014 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BrowBr00/gamelog/2014/ |access-date=2024-12-24 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> He helped the Patriots win [[Super Bowl XLIX]] over his former team, the [[Seattle Seahawks]] 28–24. In the Super Bowl, Browner recorded three tackles.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Super Bowl XLIX - New England Patriots vs. Seattle Seahawks - February 1st, 2015 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201502010sea.htm |access-date=2024-12-24 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> With 26 seconds left, he blocked [[Jermaine Kearse]] on a pick play on second and goal from the one yard line, enabling [[Malcolm Butler]] to make the [[Butler interception|game-sealing interception]].

At the start of free agency, the Patriots did not pick up a $2 million roster bonus due to him, making him a free agent eligible to sign with any team.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Reiss|first1=Mike|title=Patriots don't pick up Brandon Browner option, making him free agent|date=March 10, 2015 |url=https://www.espn.com/blog/boston/new-england-patriots/post/_/id/4778965/patriots-dont-pick-up-brandon-browner-option-making-him-a-free-agent|publisher=ESPN|access-date=March 11, 2015}}</ref>

===New Orleans Saints===
On March 12, 2015, Browner signed with the [[New Orleans Saints]].<ref>{{cite web|title=New Orleans Saints announce a number of roster moves on Thursday|url=http://www.neworleanssaints.com/news-and-events/article-1/New-Orleans-Saints-announce-a-number-of-roster-moves-on-Thursday/4583e9ce-29b0-4339-85fa-70da86b43044|work=NewOrleansSaints.com|date=March ===Seattle Seahawks (second stint)===
On April 17, 2016, Browner signed a one-year deal for the veteran minimum salary ($760,000) with his former team, the [[Seattle Seahawks]],<ref>Bob Condotta, [http://www.seattletimes.com/sports/seahawks/details-of-brandon-browners-contract-reveal-low-risk-for-seahawks/ "Details of Brandon Browner's contract reveal low risk for Seahawks "], ''[[Seattle Times]]'', April 21, 2016.</ref> reforming the original [[Legion of Boom (Seattle Seahawks)|Legion of Boom]]. Seahawks head coach [[Pete Carroll]] stated Browner would play a different role than the previous stint with the Seahawks as a hybrid corner/safety/linebacker in the nickel package. However, the Seahawks released Browner on August 29, after the team's third preseason game.<ref>{{cite web|title=Seahawks Make Roster Moves|url=http://www.seahawks.com/news/2016/08/29/seahawks-make-roster-moves|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180328115504/http://www.seahawks.com/news/2016/08/29/seahawks-make-roster-moves|url-status=dead|archive-date=March 28, 2018|website=Seahawks.com|date=August 29, 2016}}</ref>

==Legal issues==
On May 25, 2017, Browner was arrested by [[Los Angeles, California|Los Angeles]] police for possession of [[cocaine]] and being under the influence.<ref>{{cite news |work=Patriots Wire |url=https://patriotswire.usatoday.com/2017/10/20/report-brandon-browner-busted-for-cocaine-in-may/ |title=Report: Brandon Browner arrested on cocaine possession charge in May |first=Henry |last=McKenna |date=October 20, 2017 |access-date=July 13, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Report: Brandon Browner Arrested for Cocaine Possession in May| url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/2739779-report-brandon-browner-arrested-for-cocaine-possession-in-may |access-date=July 5, 2025| website=[[BleacherReport.com]]| date=October 20, 2017}}</ref>

On September 11, 2017, [[La Verne, California|La Verne]] police arrested Browner for felony suspicion of making criminal threats.<ref>{{cite web |title=Brandon Browner: Former Pro Bowl CB arrested for felony in Los Angeles| url=https://www.upi.com/Sports_News/NFL/2017/09/13/Brandon-Browner-Former-Pro-Bowl-CB-arrested-for-felony-in-Los-Angeles/5251505335887/ |access-date=July 5, 2025| website=[[UPI.com]]| date=September 13, 2017}}</ref>

On July 8, 2018, Browner was arrested by La Verne police for breaking and entering into the residence of a woman with whom he once had a relationship, and fleeing the scene after stealing a [[Rolex]] within the home.<ref>{{cite web |work=NFL.com |url=http://www.nfl.com/news/story/0ap3000000939686/article/former-nfl-corner-brandon-browner-arrested-on-felony-charges |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180709061105/http://www.nfl.com/news/story/0ap3000000939686/article/former-nfl-corner-brandon-browner-arrested-on-felony-charges |url-status=dead |archive-date=July 9, 2018 |title=Former NFL corner Brandon Browner arrested on felony charges |first=Nick |last=Shook |date=July 8, 2018 |access-date=July 13, 2018}}</ref> Two days later, he was officially charged with attempted murder and three other felonies.<ref name="Murder Charge"/> On December 4, 2018, Browner was sentenced to eight years in prison after pleading no contest to an attempted murder charge.<ref>{{cite web |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |url=https://www.latimes.com/sports/sportsnow/la-sp-brandon-browner-attempted-murder-20181204-story.html |title=Former Pro Bowler Brandon Browner pleads no contest to attempted murder |first=Nathan |last=Fenno |date=December 4, 2018 |access-date=December 4, 2018}}</ref> He became eligible for parole in November 2023.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.latimes.com/sports/story/2020-03-16/brandon-browner-prison |title=Former Pro Bowl player Brandon Browner is sent to prison for attempted murder |last=Fenno |first=Nathan |date=March 16, 2020 |website=[[Los Angeles Times]] |access-date=April 4, 2023 |quote=Browner won't be eligible for parole until November 2023, according to Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation records.}}</ref>

'''Brandon David Fields''' (born May 21, 1984) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Punter (American football)|punter]] for nine seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Michigan State Spartans football|Michigan State Spartans]], earning consensus [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] honors. He was selected by the [[Miami Dolphins]] in the seventh round of the [[2007 NFL draft]]. He also played for the [[New Orleans Saints]].

==Early life==
Fields was born in [[Southfield, Michigan]]. He attended [[St. John's Jesuit High School and Academy|St. John's Jesuit High School]] in [[Toledo, Ohio]],<ref name="DolphinsBio">{{Cite web |title=TEAM: Roster Brandon Fields Profile |url=http://www.miamidolphins.com/newsite/team/roster/playerBio.asp?docid=27205 |url-status=dead |website=MiamiDolphins.com |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090420150903/http://www.miamidolphins.com/newsite/team/roster/playerBio.asp?docid=27205 |archivedate=April 20, 2009}}</ref> and played for the St. John's Titans [[high school football]] team. During his senior season, he handled kickoff duties for the Titans football team and was a first-team all-state selection as a punter while also playing tight end.<ref name="DolphinsBio" /> Fields also lettered in basketball for St. John's.<ref name="DolphinsBio" />

==College career==
Fields attended Michigan State University, and played for the [[Michigan State Spartans football]] team from 2003 to 2006.<ref name="SpartansBio">{{Cite web |title=Player Bio: Brandon Fields |url=http://msuspartans.cstv.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/fields_brandon00.html |website=MSUSpartans.CSTV.com |accessdate=July 4, 2008}}</ref> He earned [[Brandon Fields#Awards and honors|numerous honors]] during his freshman season in 2003. He led the [[Big Ten Conference]] and was second in the nation with a 46.4-yard average.<ref name="SpartansBio" /> In a game against [[Nebraska Cornhuskers football|Nebraska]], Fields set an [[Alamo Bowl]] record with a 62-yard punt.<ref name="SpartansBio" />

Fields had the most productive season of his collegiate career as a sophomore in 2004, leading the nation with a 47.9-yard punting average.<ref name="SpartansBio" /> Honors on the season included numerous All-Big Ten and [[All-America]]n selections.<ref name="SpartansBio" /> He was also a finalist for the [[Ray Guy Award]], given annually to the nation's top punter.<ref name="SpartansBio" />

As a junior in 2005, Fields handled the kickoff duties for the first four games of the season in addition to being the team's punter.<ref name="DolphinsBio" /> He wrapped up his collegiate career with a 45.0-yard punting average as a senior.<ref name="DolphinsBio" />

On December 13, 2010, the Big Ten Conference instituted the Eddleman-Fields Punter of the Year award to honor Fields and Thomas "Dike" Eddleman, Illinois punter from 1946 to 1948.

===Awards and honors===
During his collegiate career at Michigan State, Fields earned the following honors:<ref name="SpartansBio" />

'''Freshman (2003):'''
* Mid-season [[Sports Illustrated|SI.com]] [[All-America]]n
* Second-team coaches [[List of All-Big Ten Conference football teams|All-Big Ten]]
* First-team media All-Big Ten
* First-team ''[[Sporting News]]'' Freshman All-American
* Honorable mention [[Rivals.com]] All-American
* Second-team ''Sporting News'' All-American

'''Sophomore (2004):'''
* Second-team coaches All-Big Ten
* First-team media All-Big Ten
* First-team [[Associated Press|AP]] All-American
* First-team [[Football Writers Association of America|FWAA]] All-American
* First-team Rivals.com All-American
* First-team SI.com All-American
* First-team [[Walter Camp Football Foundation|Walter Camp]] All-American
* [[Ray Guy Award]] finalist

In addition to his football accolades, Fields was an Academic All-Big Ten selection each of his four years at Michigan State.<ref name="Academic">{{Cite web |date=December 7, 2005 |title=Eighteen Spartan Football Players Earn Academic All-Big Ten Honors |url=http://msuspartans.cstv.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/120705aai.html |website=MSUSpartans.CSTV.com}}</ref>

==Professional career==

===Pre-draft===
Prior to the [[2007 NFL draft]], Fields was invited to the [[NFL Scouting Combine]] in [[Indianapolis, Indiana|Indianapolis]].<ref name="KFFLnews">{{Cite web |title=KFFL – Brandon Fields, P |url=http://www.kffl.com/player/16365/nfl/news |url-status=dead |website=KFFL.com |accessdate=July 4, 2008 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20141204164312/http://www.kffl.com/player/16365/nfl/news |archivedate=December 4, 2014}}</ref> At his [[Pro Day]] in April, Fields measured in at 6-foot-4 7/8 and 236 pounds.<ref name="KFFLnews" />

===Miami Dolphins===
Fields was drafted by the Miami Dolphins in the seventh round (225th overall) of the 2007 NFL Draft.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2007 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2007/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-11 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> The pick used to select Fields was acquired from the [[St. Louis Rams]] earlier in the offseason in exchange for punter [[Donnie Jones]].<ref name="DolphinsBio" /> Fields was the first punter drafted by the Dolphins since [[Brent Bartholomew]] in [[1999 NFL draft|1999]] and was the first rookie to handle punting duties for the team on a full-time basis since [[Reggie Roby]] in 1983.<ref name="DolphinsBio" /> On May 24, the Dolphins signed Fields to a four-year contract.<ref name="KFFLnews" />

Fields handled punting duties for the Dolphins during all 16 games of his rookie season.<ref name="DolphinsBio" /> His 77 punts averaged 43.2 yards in length, with 10 of them landing inside the opponent's 20-yard line.<ref name="DolphinsBio" /> He also served as the holder on field goals and extra points.<ref name="DolphinsBio" /> His gross average ranked seventh in the [[American Football Conference|AFC]] and led all four rookie punters in the NFL that season and has improved in all facets of his game every season since.<ref name="DolphinsBio" />

During the 2008 offseason, it was reported that new Dolphins Vice President [[Bill Parcells]] "absolutely loves Brandon Fields."<ref name="Parcells">{{Cite web |last=Armando Salguero |date=June 5, 2008 |title=The Tuna speaks to ME (and others) |url=http://miamiherald.typepad.com/dolphins_in_depth/2008/06/the-tuna-speaks.html |website=Herald.com}}</ref> The team did not pursue competition for him that offseason or since.<ref name="Parcells" />

On December 27, 2013, the NFL announced Fields as a selection for the [[2014 Pro Bowl]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Hal Habib |date=December 27, 2013 |title=Four Miami Dolphins named to Pro Bowl: Mike Pouncey, Cameron Wake, Brent Grimes and Brandon Fields |work=The Palm Beach Post |url=http://www.palmbeachpost.com/news/sports/football/four-miami-dolphins-named-to-pro-bowl-mike-pouncey/ncW8d/ |accessdate=December 28, 2013}}</ref>

Fields was released on September 1, 2015.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kelly |first=Omar |title=Miami Dolphins release Pro Bowl punter Brandon Fields |date=September 2015 |url=http://www.sun-sentinel.com/sports/miami-dolphins/sfl-miami-dolphins-plan-to-release-pro-bowl-punter-brandon-fields-20150901-story.html |publisher=Sun Sentinel |accessdate=1 September 2015}}</ref>

===New Orleans Saints===
Fields signed with the [[New Orleans Saints]] on October 6, 2015, to replace [[Thomas Morstead]] while he recovered from a strained quadriceps. Fields played in two games, and was then released on October 20, 2015.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Terrell |first=Katherine |title=New Orleans Saints release punter Brandon Fields, source says |work=NOLA.com |url=http://www.nola.com/saints/index.ssf/2015/10/new_orleans_saints_release_pun_1.html |accessdate=20 October 2015}}</ref>

===Retirement===
On September 29, 2017, Fields announced his retirement from the NFL.<ref>{{Cite web |date=September 29, 2017 |title=Former Dolphins punter Brandon Fields retires from the NFL |url=http://www.sun-sentinel.com/sports/miami-dolphins/fl-sp-dolphins-brandon-fields-retiring-20170928-story.html |website=Sun-Sentinel.com}}</ref>

==Personal life==
His wife, Katie, whom he married during the 2008 offseason, earned her degree in chiropractic medicine at [[Palmer College of Chiropractic]] in [[Port Orange, Florida]].
He is part owner of Inside The Five Brewery in Sylvania, Ohio and Perrysburg, Ohio.

'''Brandon Lee Frye''' (born January 23, 1983) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[offensive tackle]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[Houston Texans]] in the fifth round of the [[2007 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2007 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2007/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-11 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He played [[college football]] for the [[Virginia Tech Hokies football|Virginia Tech Hokies]].

Frye was also a member of the [[Miami Dolphins]] and [[Seattle Seahawks]].

==College career==
Frye played [[college football]] for the [[Virginia Tech Hokies football|Virginia Tech Hokies]]. After playing sparingly his first three seasons, he earned the starting left job at the end of the [[2005 Virginia Tech Hokies football team|2005 season]] for the [[2006 Gator Bowl|Toyota Gator Bowl]] against [[2005 Louisville Cardinals football team|Louisville]] after [[Jimmy Martin (American football)|Jimmy Martin]] was injured. He retained the starting job during the [[2006 Virginia Tech Hokies football team|2006 season]] and started all but two games his final year with the Hokies.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hokiesports.com/football/notes/12302006.pdf|title=Hokies and Bulldogs to clash in the Dome|accessdate=September 11, 2007|pages=11|publisher=hokiesports.com|archive-date=March 3, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303182648/http://www.hokiesports.com/football/notes/12302006.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Professional career==
===Houston Texans===
Frye was selected by the [[Houston Texans]] in the fifth round, with the 163rd overall pick, of the [[2007 NFL draft]].<ref name="Pfr">{{Cite web |title=Brandon Frye Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/F/FryeBr21.htm |access-date=24 August 2024 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He officially signed with the team on July 26. He was waived on September 1 and signed to the Texans' practice squad on September 3. Frye was promoted to the active roster on October 31, 2007.<ref name="Pfr" /> However, he did not appear in any games for the Texans and became a free agent after the 2007 season.<ref name="Pfr" /><ref name="transactions">{{cite web | url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/transactions/f/frye00050.html | title=Brandon Frye NFL Transactions | publisher=Pro Football Archives | accessdate=24 August 2024}}</ref>

Frye re-signed with the Texans on March 28, 2008. He was waived on September 2 and signed to the practice squad on September 4, 2008.<ref name="Pfr" />

===Miami Dolphins===
On November 5, 2008, Frye was signed to the [[Miami Dolphins]]' active roster off of the Texans' practice squad. He appeared in seven games for the Dolphins during the 2008 season. He was waived by the Dolphins on September 5, 2009.<ref name="Pfr" />

===Seattle Seahawks===
Frye signed with the [[Seattle Seahawks]] September 6, 2009. He played in four games, starting three, for the Seahawks in 2009 before being placed on injured reserve on October 13, 2009.<ref name="Pfr" /> He became a free agent after the season.<ref name="transactions"/>

==Personal life==
He currently resides in the Washington, D.C. metro area.{{cn|date=August 2024}}

'''Brandon Coutu''' (born September 29, 1984) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[placekicker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[Seattle Seahawks]] in the seventh round of the [[2008 NFL draft]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Georgia Bulldogs football|Georgia Bulldogs]].

He was also a member of the [[Las Vegas Locomotives]], [[Jacksonville Jaguars]], [[Buffalo Bills]], and [[Omaha Nighthawks]].

==College career==
At the [[University of Georgia]], he kicked three field goals of over 50 yards, his longest was 58 yards.  He never missed a PAT at Georgia and was the first kicker in Georgia history to have over 80% field goal accuracy.  All these things were accomplished after turning down scholarships at other schools for soccer and being a walk-on on Georgia's football team.

==Professional career==

===Seattle Seahawks===
Coutu was drafted by the [[Seattle Seahawks]] in the seventh round of the [[2008 NFL draft]] with the 235th overall pick. He was one of only two kickers picked by NFL teams in that draft.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2008 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2008/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-12 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He was waived by the team on September 5, 2009.

Coutu was re-signed by the Seahawks on July 30, 2011, to replace [[Olindo Mare]]. He was released on August 20.

===Las Vegas Locomotives===
On August 25, 2011, Coutu signed with the [[Las Vegas Locomotives]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Personnel Transaction Notice - August 25, 2011|url=http://www.ufl-football.com/news/personnel-transaction-notice-august-25-2011|work=United Football League|accessdate=27 August 2011|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110912023845/http://www.ufl-football.com/news/personnel-transaction-notice-august-25-2011|archivedate=12 September 2011}}</ref>

===Jacksonville Jaguars (first stint)===
On December 12, 2011, Coutu was signed to the [[Jacksonville Jaguars]] practice squad.

===Buffalo Bills===
Coutu signed with the [[Buffalo Bills]] on December 28, 2011, to replace the injured [[Rian Lindell]] and [[Dave Rayner]]. He was Buffalo's third kicker of the season.<ref>[http://www.democratandchronicle.com/article/20111228/SPORTS03/111228018/Bills-sign-kicker-Brandon-Coutu-replace-Dave-Rayner-?odyssey=nav%7Chead Bills sign kicker Brandon Coutu to replace Dave Rayner]</ref> He attempted his first NFL field goal on a New Years Day game against the [[New England Patriots]], but missed. He was released following the season.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://insider.espn.com/nfl/freeagency/|title = Free Agent Tracker}}</ref>

===Jacksonville Jaguars (second stint)===
He re-signed with the Jaguars in May 2012.<ref>http://www.cbssports.com/nfl/rapid-reports/post/19043638 {{Dead link|date=February 2022}}</ref> He was waived on July 17 to make room for newly signed [[Josh Scobee]].

===Omaha Nighthawks===
Coutu played for the [[Omaha Nighthawks]] in 2012.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.statscrew.com/football/stats/p-coutubra001 | title=Brandon Coutu | publisher=statscrew.com | accessdate=May 19, 2024}}</ref>

'''Brandon Lavar Flowers''' (born February 18, 1986) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[cornerback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Virginia Tech Hokies football|Virginia Tech Hokies]], and was selected by the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] in the second round of the [[2008 NFL draft]].

==Early life==
Flowers played [[high school football]] while attending [[Atlantic Community High School]], where he earned first-team all-area and all-conference honors. He was teammates with [[Omar Jacobs]] and [[David Clowney]]. Flowers then attended [[Hargrave Military Academy]] for prep school in 2003.<ref name="Brandon Flowers, #24, Cornerback, Kansas City Chiefs">{{cite web|url=http://www.kcchiefs.com/player/brandon_flowers/ |title=Brandon Flowers, #24, Cornerback, Kansas City Chiefs |access-date=October 30, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080730234948/http://www.kcchiefs.com/player/brandon_flowers/ |archive-date=July 30, 2008 |url-status=dead }}</ref> At Hargrave, he was teammates with [[Jonathan Hefney]], [[Brian Soi]], [[DJ Ware]], and [[Justin Harper (American football)|Justin Harper]]. He also starred in [[high school basketball|basketball]] and [[track and field|track]].

Although considered a three-star recruit, Flowers was not listed among the nation's top cornerback prospects by ''[[Rivals.com]]''.<ref>{{Citation |url=https://sports.yahoo.com/ncaa/football/recruiting/player-Brandon-Flowers-23774 |work=Rivals.com |title=Brandon Flowers Recruiting Profile |access-date=February 18, 2010 |archive-date=December 13, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191213135932/https://sports.yahoo.com/ncaa/football/recruiting/player-Brandon-Flowers-23774 |url-status=live }}.</ref>

==College career==
[[File:Brandon Flowers.jpg|thumb|left|Flowers with [[Virginia Tech Hokies football|Virginia Tech]] in 2007]]
Flowers attended [[Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University|Virginia Tech]], where he majored in [[Sociology]]. In 2004; he did not play in the season opener vs. Southern California, but made a spectacular interception for a 38-yard return the following week vs. Western Michigan. He suffered a fractured right fibula later in the contest and missed the rest of the season. Flowers returned to action in 2005, posting 20 tackles (13 solo) with four pass deflections, 1 1/2 stops behind the line of scrimmage, and an interception.

As a sophomore in 2006, Flowers took over the boundary cornerback spot, going on to start his final 27 games with the Hokies. He earned All-American second-team and All-Atlantic Coast Conference first-team honors, leading the league with 21 passes defended, breaking up 18 throws and picking off three others. He totaled 51 tackles (29 solo) with 3.5 sacks and 7.5 stops for losses. He also caused a fumble and did not allow an opponent to catch any passes in three games.

As a junior in 2007, Flowers again received All-American and All-ACC recognition. In 2007, Flowers intercepted five passes and deflected nine others; he also ranked third on the team with 86 tackles (56 solo), including eight stops behind the line of scrimmage.

In 41 games at Virginia Tech, Flowers made 28 starts at cornerback, making 158 tackles (99 solo) with 3.5 sacks for minus-28 yards, 17 stops for losses of 71 yards and six quarterback pressures. He caused and recovered a fumble, deflected 32 passes, and intercepted 10 others for 172 yards in returns and two touchdowns. He also led the [[Atlantic Coast Conference]] in passes broken up (18) and passes defended (21).

Flowers decided to forgo his final year of eligibility to enter the [[2008 NFL draft]].<ref>{{cite news|url=http://msn.foxsports.com/cfb/story/7647258|title=Virginia Tech's Flowers declaring for NFL draft|agency=Associated Press|work=Fox Sports|date=January 7, 2008|access-date=January 8, 2008|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080115053909/http://msn.foxsports.com/cfb/story/7647258|archive-date=January 15, 2008}}</ref>

==Professional career==
===Pre-draft===
[[NFL.com]] ranked Flowers as the sixth best cornerback prospect in the draft and projected that he would be selected in the first or second round.<ref>{{cite web| title=Draft's Top Cornerbacks| url=https://www.nfl.com/news/draft-s-top-cornerbacks-09000d5d807d2841| access-date=April 21, 2025| website=NFL.com| date=April 6, 2012| archive-date=February 17, 2025| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250217034628/https://www.nfl.com/news/draft-s-top-cornerbacks-09000d5d807d2841| url-status=live}}</ref> ''[[Sports Illustrated]]'' ranked Flowers as the eighth best cornerback prospect in the draft and described him as an "opportunistic cornerback with solid ball skills".<ref>{{cite news|title=2008 NFL Draft - Brandon Flowers|url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/football/2008/draft/players/9086.html|work=Sports Illustrated|date=November 12, 2012|url-status=bot: unknown|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121112171234/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/football/2008/draft/players/9086.html|archive-date=November 12, 2012}}</ref>

===Kansas City Chiefs===
====2008====
The [[Kansas City Chiefs]] selected Flowers in the second round (35th overall) of the [[2008 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2008 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2008/draft.htm |access-date=May 11, 2023 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en |archive-date=November 3, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181103014038/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2008/draft.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> He was the sixth cornerback drafted and the first of two cornerbacks selected by the Chiefs in 2008, along with fifth-round pick (140th overall) [[Brandon Carr]]. He was the highest selected Virginia Tech Hokies' defender since [[2004 NFL draft|2004]] first-round pick (eighth overall) [[DeAngelo Hall]]. Patrick Surtain had recommended to the Chiefs that they should draft Flowers and also kept track of their interest into selecting him. He had known Patrick Surtain for more than a decade as Surtain's brother married Flowers first cousin.<ref name="Surtain"/>
[[File:Flowers and Morgan.JPG|thumb|left|Flowers (left) with the Chiefs]]

On July 23, 2008, the [[2008 Kansas City Chiefs season|Kansas City Chiefs]] signed Flowers to a four–year, $4.72 million [[rookie]] [[contract]] that included a [[signing bonus]] of $1.52 million.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.kansascity.com/385/story/717333.html |title=www.kansascity.com | 07/23/2008 | Chiefs reach deal with 2nd-round pick Flowers |access-date=July 23, 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080729063634/http://www.kansascity.com/385/story/717333.html |archive-date=July 29, 2008 }}</ref><ref name="spotrac">{{cite web| title=Spotrac.com: Brandon Flowers contract| url=https://www.spotrac.com/nfl/player/_/id/4409/brandon-flowers| access-date=April 20, 2025| website=Spotrac.com| archive-date=September 16, 2024| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240916083941/https://www.spotrac.com/nfl/player/_/id/4409/brandon-flowers| url-status=live}}</ref>

During training camp, he competed to be the No. 2 starting cornerback against fellow rookie Brandon Carr and [[Tyron Brackenridge]] following the departure of [[Ty Law]].<ref name="Surtain">{{cite web| title=Cornerback situation a family affair for the Chiefs| url=https://www.examiner.net/story/sports/2008/07/31/cornerback-situation-family-affair-for/45488284007/| access-date=April 20, 2025| website=examiner.net| date=July 21, 2008}}</ref> Head coach [[Herm Edwards]] named Flowers and [[Patrick Surtain]] the starting cornerbacks to begin the season.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.espn.com/espn/wire?section=nfl&id=3512296|title=Flowers flanking 'cousin' in Chiefs secondary|work=ESPN.com|agency=Associated Press|archive-date=December 15, 2018|access-date=July 21, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181215175150/http://www.espn.com/espn/wire?section=nfl&id=3512296|url-status=live}}</ref>

On September 7, 2008, Flowers made his professional regular season debut and earned his first career start in the Kansas City Chiefs' season-opener at the [[2008 New England Patriots season|New England Patriots]] and made six combined tackles (five solo) during a 10–17 loss. On October 26, 2008, Flowers had eight combined tackles (five solo), made two pass deflections, a season-high two interceptions, and scored the first touchdown of his career during a 28–24 loss at the [[2008 New York Jets season|New York Jets]]. He had his first career interception on a pass by [[Brett Favre]] to wide receiver [[Jerricho Cotchery]] and returned it for 27–yards during the first quarter. In the fourth quarter he had his first career pick-six after picking off a pass by Brett Favre to wide receiver [[Chansi Stuckey]] and returned it 91–yards for a touchdown. He was inactive for two games (Weeks 10–11) due to a thigh injury.<ref>{{cite web| title=Injury Update: Week 10| url=https://fftoday.com/nfl/08_injury_wk10.html| access-date=April 21, 2025| website=fftoday.com}}</ref> On Week 15, he set a season-high with ten solo tackles during a 21–22 loss against the [[2008 San Diego Chargers season|San Diego Chargers]].
He finished the season with 68 combined tackles (61 solo), 13 pass break-ups, two interceptions, two fumble recoveries, one forced fumble, and a touchdown in 14 games and 13 starts.<ref name="career">{{cite web| title=Pro-Football-Reference: Brandon Flowers Career Overview| url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/F/FlowBr99.htm| access-date=April 21, 2025| website=Pro-Football-Reference.com| archive-date=December 15, 2024| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241215154616/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/F/FlowBr99.htm| url-status=live}}</ref>

====2009====
He entered training camp slated as the No. 1 starting cornerback under defensive coordinator [[Clancy Pendergast]] following the departure of [[Patrick Surtain]]. The Chiefs' new head coach [[Todd Haley]] named Flowers and Brandon Carr the starting cornerbacks to begin the season.<ref>{{cite web| title=Ourlads.com: Kansas City Chiefs Depth Chart (10/01/2009)| url=https://www.ourlads.com/nfldepthcharts/archive/41/kc| access-date=April 21, 2025| website=Ourlads.com}}</ref>

He was inactive for the [[2009 Kansas City Chiefs season|Kansas City Chiefs']] 24–38 loss at the [[2009 Baltimore Ravens season|Baltimore Ravens]] in Week 1 due to a shoulder injury.<ref>{{cite web| title=Chiefs Cassel moving better| url=https://www.cjonline.com/story/news/education/2009/09/16/chiefs-cassel-moving-better/16593711007/| access-date=April 21, 2025| website=cjonline.com| date=September 16, 2009}}</ref> In Week 3, Flowers set a season-high with seven combined tackles (six solo) and made one pass deflection during a 14–34 loss against the [[2009 Philadelphia Eagles season|Philadelphia Eagles]]. In Week 14, Flowers made six combined tackles (three solo), one pass deflection, and intercepted a pass by [[Ryan Fitzpatrick]] to wide receiver [[Lee Evans (American football)|Lee Evans]] during a 10–16 loss to the [[2009 Buffalo Bills season|Buffalo Bills]].<ref>{{cite web| title=Buffalo Bills at Kansas City - December 13th, 2009| url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200912130kan.htm| access-date=April 21, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com| archive-date=February 27, 2018| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180227153520/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200912130kan.htm| url-status=live}}</ref> The following week, he had three solo tackles, one pass deflection, and intercepted a pass thrown by [[Brady Quinn]] to wide receiver [[Mohamed Massaquoi]] during a 34–41 loss against the [[2009 Cleveland Browns season|Cleveland Browns]] in Week 15. On January 3, 2010, Flowers made four solo tackles, set a season-high with four pass deflections, and set a career-high with his fifth interception of the season on a pass by [[Kyle Orton]] to wide receiver [[Jabar Gaffney]] during a 44–24 win at the [[2009 Denver Broncos season|Denver Broncos]].<ref>{{cite web| title=Kansas City Chiefs at Denver Broncos - January 3rd, 2010| url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201001030den.htm| access-date=April 21, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com| archive-date=February 27, 2018| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180227153500/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201001030den.htm| url-status=live}}</ref> Despite playing nearly all the 2009 season with a hurt shoulder, Flowers finished the season with a total of 65 combined tackles (58 solo), a career-high 23 pass deflections, a career-high five interceptions, made two forced fumbles, and had two fumble recoveries in 15 games and 15 starts.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Teicher|first1=Adam|title=Flowers working on breakout season - KansasCity.com|url=http://www.kansascity.com/2010/04/02/1853697/flowers-working-to-have-a-breakout.html|work=Kansas City Star|date=April 9, 2010|url-status=bot: unknown|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100409010231/http://www.kansascity.com/2010/04/02/1853697/flowers-working-to-have-a-breakout.html|archive-date=April 9, 2010}}</ref>

====2010====
On January 14, 2010, the [[2010 Kansas City Chiefs season|Kansas City Chiefs]] hired [[Romeo Crennel]] to be their defensive coordinator after deciding not to re-sign Clancy Pendergast. Head coach Todd Haley retained Flowers and Carr as the starting cornerbacks and named rookie [[Javier Arenas (American football)|Javier Arenas]] the starting nickelback.<ref>{{cite web| title=Ourlads.com: Kansas City Chiefs Depth Chart (09/05/2010)| url=https://www.ourlads.com/nfldepthcharts/archive/111/kc| access-date=April 21, 2025| website=Ourlads.com}}</ref>

On September 19, 2010, Flowers made three solo tackles, one pass deflection, and intercepted a pass by [[Seneca Wallace]] to wide receiver [[Chansi Stuckey]] and returned it 16–14 for a touchdown during a 16–14 victory at the [[2010 Cleveland Browns season|Cleveland Browns]]. In Week 3, he had two solo tackles, set a season-high with three pass deflections, and intercepted a pass by [[Alex Smith]] to wide receiver [[Michael Crabtree]] during a 31–10 win against the [[2010 San Francisco 49ers season|San Francisco 49ers]]. In Week 11, he had seven combined tackles (five solo) and made two pass deflections before exiting in the third quarter of a 31–13 win against the [[2010 Arizona Cardinals season|Arizona Cardinals]] due to an injury to his hamstring. He was inactive for the Chiefs' 42–24 win at the [[2010 Seattle Seahawks season|Seattle Seahawks]] in Week 12 due to his hamstring injury.<ref>{{cite web| title=Brandon Flowers' Injury Keeps Him Out Of Chiefs Practice Again| url=https://www.arrowheadpride.com/2010/11/25/1836278/brandon-flowers-injury-keeps-him-out-of-chiefs-practice-again| access-date=April 21, 2025| website=arrowheadpride.com| author=Joel Thorman| date=November 25, 2010| archive-date=September 23, 2023| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230923175356/https://www.arrowheadpride.com/2010/11/25/1836278/brandon-flowers-injury-keeps-him-out-of-chiefs-practice-again| url-status=live}}</ref> In Week 16, he set a season-high with seven solo tackles as the Chiefs defeated the [[2010 Tennessee Titans season|Tennessee Titans]] 34–14. He finished the season with 65 combined tackles (56 solo), 14 pass deflections, and two interceptions, and one touchdown in 15 games and 15 starts.<ref name="career"/> During the 2010 season, he helped lead the Chiefs to the 14th ranked defense (in yards per game), after finishing 30th the previous season, and helped lead the Chiefs to their first division title since [[2003 Kansas City Chiefs season|2003]].

The [[2010 Kansas City Chiefs season|Kansas City Chiefs]] finished the [[2010 NFL season]] first in the [[AFC West]] with a 10–6 record. On January 9, 2011, Flowers started in his first career playoff game and made three solo tackles and one pass deflection during a 7–30 loss against the [[2010 Baltimore Ravens season|Baltimore Ravens]] in the AFC Wild-Card Game.

====2011====
On September 16, 2011, the [[2011 Kansas City Chiefs season|Kansas City Chiefs]] signed Flowers to a five–year, $49.35 million contract extension that included $22.00 million guaranteed and an initial signing bonus of $10.00 million.<ref name="Roto Wire">{{cite web|last=Siciliano|first=Andrew|title=Direct TV Redzone|url=http://www.rotoworld.com/player/nfl/4733/brandon-flowers|work=Direct TV|publisher=Roto Wire|access-date=September 16, 2011}}</ref><ref name="spotrac"/>

On September 25, 2011, Flowers set a season-high with eight combined tackles (six solo), made one pass deflection, and intercepted a pass by Phillip Rivers to wide receiver [[Malcom Floyd]] during a 17–20 loss at the [[2011 San Diego Chargers season|San Diego Chargers]]. On October 23, 2011, Flowers made three solo tackles, three pass deflections, two interceptions, and returned one for a touchdown during a 28–0 victory at the [[2011 Oakland Raiders season|Oakland Raiders]]. He intercepted a pass thrown by [[Carson Palmer]] to wide receiver [[Denarius Moore]] in the fourth quarter and returned it 38–yards for a touchdown.<ref>{{cite web| title=Kansas City Chiefs at Oakland Raiders - October 23rd, 2011| url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201110230rai.htm| access-date=April 21, 2025| website=Pro-Football-Reference.com| archive-date=January 6, 2018| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180106063728/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201110230rai.htm| url-status=live}}</ref> The following week, he recorded five combined tackles (four solo) and set a season-high with four pass deflections as the Chiefs defeated the [[2011 San Diego Chargers season|San Diego Chargers]] in overtime 23–20 in Week 8. On December 12, 2011, the Chiefs fired head coach Todd Haley after leading his team to a 5–8 record. Defensive coordinator Romeo Crennel was appointed interim head coach for the remainder of the season.<ref name="Firing">{{cite web | title=Haley relieved of duties | url=http://www.kcchiefs.com/news/article-2/HALEY-RELIEVED-OF-DUTIES/9f2d029b-c450-48cb-9791-8038582a3270 | date=December 12, 2011 | access-date=December 12, 2011 | publisher=Kansas City Chiefs | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120107051055/http://www.kcchiefs.com/news/article-2/HALEY-RELIEVED-OF-DUTIES/9f2d029b-c450-48cb-9791-8038582a3270 | archive-date=January 7, 2012 | url-status=dead }}</ref> He started in all 16 games for the first time in his career and made 59 combined tackles (44 solo), 20 pass deflections, four interceptions, and one touchdown.<ref name="career"/>

====2012====
Defensive coordinator Romeo Crennel was promoted to head coach entering the [[2012 NFL season]]. He entered training camp slated as the No. 1 starting cornerback, but missed the majority of camp after injuring his foot. He was named the No. 1 starting cornerback to begin the season and was paired with [[Stanford Routt]], following the departure of [[Brandon Carr]] who joined the [[2012 Dallas Cowboys season|Dallas Cowboys]] via free agency.

He was inactive due to an injury to the heel of his foot and remained on the sideline for the [[2012 Kansas City Chiefs season|Kansas City Chiefs']] home-opener against the [[2012 Atlanta Falcons season|Atlanta Falcons]] as they lost 24–40. In Week 4, he made three solo tackles, set a season-high with two pass deflections, and intercepted a pass by Phillip Rivers to wide receiver [[Robert Meachem]] during a 20–37 loss to the [[2012 San Diego Chargers season|San Diego Chargers]]. In Week 12, he tied his season-high with four solo tackles, made one pass deflection, and picked off a pass thrown by [[Peyton Manning]] to [[Eric Decker]] during a 9–17 loss to the [[2012 Denver Broncos season|Denver Broncos]].<ref>{{cite web| title=Denver Broncos at Kansas City Chiefs - November 25th, 2012| url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201211010sdg.htm| access-date=April 21, 2025| website=Pro-Football-Reference.com| archive-date=November 14, 2022| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221114034901/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201211010sdg.htm| url-status=live}}</ref> In Week 16, he recorded four solo tackles, had one pass deflection, and had his first career sack on [[Andrew Luck]] for a two–yard loss as the Chiefs lost 13–20 to the [[2012 Indianapolis Colts season|Indianapolis Colts]].<ref>{{cite web| title=Indianapolis Colts at Kansas City Chiefs - December 23rd, 2012| url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201212230kan.htm| access-date=April 21, 2025| website=Pro-Football-Reference.com| archive-date=February 27, 2018| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180227153455/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201212230kan.htm| url-status=live}}</ref> He finished the season with 48 combined tackles (40 solo), 12 pass deflections, three interceptions, one forced fumble, and one sack in 15 games and 15 starts.<ref>{{cite web| title=Pro-Football-Reference: Brandon Flowers Game Logs (2012)| url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/F/FlowBr99.htm| access-date=April 21, 2025| website=Pro-Football-Reference.com| archive-date=December 15, 2024| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241215154616/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/F/FlowBr99.htm| url-status=live}}</ref> On December 31, 2012, the Chiefs fired head coach Romeo Crennel after they finished the [[2012 NFL season]] with a 2–14 record.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://fansided.com/2012/12/31/report-kansas-city-chiefs-fire-romeo-crennel-but-keep-scott-pioli/ |last=Hill |first=Josh |date=December 31, 2012 |access-date=December 31, 2012 |title=Report: Kansas City Chiefs Fire Romeo Crennel, But Keep Scott Pioli |publisher=FanSided.Com Sports Network |archive-date=July 8, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130708073052/http://fansided.com/2012/12/31/report-kansas-city-chiefs-fire-romeo-crennel-but-keep-scott-pioli/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

====2013====
Throughout training camp, he competed to retain his job as a starting cornerback against  [[Sean Smith (cornerback)|Sean Smith]] and [[Dunta Robinson]] under new defensive coordinator [[Bob Sutton (American football)|Bob Sutton]]. Head coach [[Andy Reid]] named him the No. 1 starting cornerback to begin the season and paired him with Sean Smith with Dunta Robinson and rookie [[Marcus Cooper (American football)|Marcus Cooper]] serving as backups.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.ourlads.com/nfldepthcharts/archive/150/KC| title=Ourlads.com: Kansas City Chiefs' depth chart: 09/05/2013| access-date=October 25, 2017| website=ourlads.com| archive-date=June 26, 2018| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180626030419/http://www.ourlads.com/nfldepthcharts/archive/150/KC| url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web| title=Kansas City Chiefs depth chart: 53-man roster edition| url=https://www.arrowheadpride.com/2013/8/31/4680632/kansas-city-chiefs-depth-chart-53-man-roster-edition| access-date=April 21, 2025| website=arrowheadpride.com| author=Joel Thorman| date=August 31, 2013| archive-date=December 25, 2024| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241225102231/https://www.arrowheadpride.com/2013/8/31/4680632/kansas-city-chiefs-depth-chart-53-man-roster-edition| url-status=live}}</ref>

On September 8, 2013, Flowers started in the [[2013 Kansas City Chiefs season|Kansas City Chiefs']] season-opener at the [[2013 Jacksonville Jaguars season|Jacksonville Jaguars]] and made four solo tackles, set a season-high with two pass deflections, and intercepted a pass by [[Blaine Gabbert]] to wide receiver [[Cecil Shorts]] during a 28–2 victory. The following week, Flowers set a season-high with ten solo tackles during a 17–16 win against the [[2013 Dallas Cowboys season|Dallas Cowboys]] in Week 2. In Week 3, he made two solo tackles before exiting in the first quarter of a 26–16 win at the [[2013 Philadelphia Eagles season|Philadelphia Eagles]] due his sprained knee.<ref>{{cite web| title=Brandon Flowers day to day| url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/9713354/brandon-flowers-kansas-city-chiefs-knee-inflammation| access-date=April 21, 2025| website=ESPN| author=Adam Teicher| date=September 23, 2013}}</ref> He was inactive for the Chiefs' 31–7 win against the [[2013 New York Giants season|New York Giants]].<ref>{{cite web| title=Brandon Flowers' injury will keep him out for Raiders-Chiefs game| url=https://www.arrowheadpride.com/2013/10/13/4833882/brandon-flowers-injury-raiders-chiefs-game| access-date=April 21, 2025| website=arrowheadpride.com| author=Adam Teicher| date=October 13, 2013| archive-date=March 21, 2023| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230321202842/https://www.arrowheadpride.com/2013/10/13/4833882/brandon-flowers-injury-raiders-chiefs-game| url-status=live}}</ref> He was inactive as the Chiefs defeated the [[2013 Oakland Raiders season|Oakland Raiders]] 24–7 in Week 5. He finished the [[2013 NFL season]] with a career-high 68 combined tackles (63 solo), eight pass deflections, one interception, and one sack in 13 games and 13 starts.<ref name="career"/>

On June 13, 2014, the [[2014 Kansas City Chiefs season|Kansas City Chiefs]] officially released Flowers.<ref>{{cite web|title=Brandon Flowers released by Kansas City Chiefs|url=https://www.nfl.com/news/brandon-flowers-released-by-kansas-city-chiefs-0ap2000000358463|website=NFL.com|access-date=June 4, 2024|archive-date=June 24, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240624093455/https://www.nfl.com/news/brandon-flowers-released-by-kansas-city-chiefs-0ap2000000358463|url-status=live}}</ref> The release saved the Chiefs $7.25 million in cap space in [[2014 NFL season|2014]] and $7.50 million in [[2015 NFL season|2015]]. It was reported that Flowers release was, in part, due to his unhappiness with having to play mostly in the slot under new defensive coordinator Bob Sutton. It was also speculated Flowers, standing at 5'9", didn't fit the physical aspects the New Chiefs' General Manager [[John Dorsey (American football)|John Dorsey]] typically favored, as he preferred taller cornerbacks.<ref>{{cite web| title=Brandon Flowers released by the Kansas City Chiefs| url=https://www.arrowheadpride.com/2014/6/13/5772066/brandon-flowers-released-kansas-city-chiefs| access-date=April 21, 2025| website=arrowheadpride.com| date=June 13, 2014| archive-date=September 21, 2023| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230921233135/https://www.arrowheadpride.com/2014/6/13/5772066/brandon-flowers-released-kansas-city-chiefs| url-status=live}}</ref>

===San Diego Chargers===
====2014====
On June 24, 2014, the [[San Diego Chargers]] signed Flowers to a one–year, $3.00 million contract that included a signing bonus of $1.50 million.<ref>{{cite news|title=Chargers agree to deal with CB Brandon Flowers|url=https://www.espn.com/espn/wire?section=nfl&id=11130876|access-date=June 25, 2014|agency=Associated Press|work=ESPN.com|date=June 24, 2014|archive-date=January 10, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170110085940/http://www.espn.com/espn/wire?section=nfl&id=11130876|url-status=live}}</ref> His decision was influenced by the opportunity to play against the Chiefs.<ref name="n143">{{cite web | title=Brandon Flowers had Chiefs in mind when joining Bolts | website=NFL.com | date=2014-06-25 | url=https://www.nfl.com/news/brandon-flowers-had-chiefs-in-mind-when-joining-bolts-0ap2000000361716 | access-date=2025-01-13 | archive-date=July 21, 2024 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240721210502/https://www.nfl.com/news/brandon-flowers-had-chiefs-in-mind-when-joining-bolts-0ap2000000361716 | url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.utsandiego.com/news/2014/Jun/30/chargers-brandon-flowers-eric-weddle-eddie-royal/|title=Chargers veterans sold Brandon Flowers|first=Michael|last=Gehlken|work=U-T San Diego|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140701123226/http://www.utsandiego.com/news/2014/Jun/30/chargers-brandon-flowers-eric-weddle-eddie-royal/|archive-date=July 1, 2014}}</ref> Throughout training camp, he competed against [[Shareece Wright]] and [[Jason Verrett]] to be a starting cornerback under defensive coordinator [[John Pagano]]. Head coach [[Mike McCoy (American football coach)|Mike McCoy]] named him the No. 1 starting cornerback and paired him with Shareece Wright to begin the season.<ref>{{cite web| title=San Diego Chargers depth chart: Jason Verrett backup cornerback| url=https://www.si.com/nfl/2014/08/07/san-diego-chargers-2014-depth-chart| access-date=April 21, 2025| website=Sports Illustrated| date=August 4, 2014}}</ref>

[[File:Brandon Flowers (Chargers).jpg|thumb|Flowers in 2014]]
On September 8, 2014, Flowers started in the San Diego Chargers' season-opener at the [[2014 Arizona Cardinals season|Arizona Cardinals]] and set a season-high with seven combined tackles (six solo) during a 17–18 loss. He was inactive for the Chargers' 30–21 victory against the [[2014 Seattle Seahawks season|Seattle Seahawks]] in Week 2 due to a groin injury.<ref>{{cite web| title=San Diego Chargers CB Brandon Flowers could miss Seahawks game| url=https://www.boltsfromtheblue.com/2014/9/12/6141099/san-diego-chargers-cb-brandon-flowers-could-miss-seahawks-game| access-date=April 21, 2025| website=boltsfromtheblue.com| date=September 12, 2014| archive-date=December 9, 2022| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221209053322/https://www.boltsfromtheblue.com/2014/9/12/6141099/san-diego-chargers-cb-brandon-flowers-could-miss-seahawks-game| url-status=live}}</ref> On September 28, 2014, Flowers made six solo tackles, one pass deflection, and picked off a pass by [[Blake Bortles]] to wide receiver [[Cecil Shorts]] during a 33–14 win against the [[2014 Jacksonville Jaguars season|Jacksonville Jaguars]]. On October 5, 2014, he had one solo tackle, set a season-high with two pass deflections, and intercepted a pass by [[Geno Smith]] to wide receiver [[Greg Salas]] as the Chargers defeated the [[2014 New York Jets season|New York Jets]] 31–0. In Week 7, Flowers recorded three combined tackles (one solo) before he exited in the third quarter of a 20–23 loss against his former team, the [[2014 Kansas City Chiefs season|Kansas City Chiefs]], after suffering a [[concussion]] in a collision with running back [[Jamaal Charles|Jamal Charles]]. He remained inactive for the Chargers' 21–35 loss at the [[2014 Denver Broncos season|Denver Broncos]] on [[Thursday Night Football]] in Week 8 as he remained in concussion protocol.<ref>{{cite web| title=Chargers' Brandon Flowers out Thursday vs. Broncos with concussion| url=https://www.si.com/nfl/2014/10/23/san-diego-padres-brandon-flowers-concussion-out| access-date=April 21, 2025| website=Sports Illustrated| date=October 22, 2014}}</ref> In Week 12, Flowers had one solo tackle, two pass deflections, and intercepted a pass by [[Shaun Hill]] to tight end [[Jared Cook]] during a 27–24 victory against the [[2014 St. Louis Rams season|St. Louis Rams]]. He finished his first season in San Diego recording 52 combined tackles (48 solo), ten pass deflections, three interceptions, in 14 games played.

====2015====
On March 8, 2015, the [[2015 San Diego Chargers season|San Diego Chargers]] signed Flowers to a four–year, $36.40 million contract extension that included $20.50 million guaranteed, $18.00 million guaranteed upon signing, and an initial [[signing bonus]] of $8.00 million.<ref>{{cite web|work=NFL.com|url=https://www.nfl.com/news/brandon-flowers-chargers-agree-to-4-year-36m-deal-0ap3000000477279|title=Brandon Flowers, Chargers agree to 4-year, $36M deal|first=Gregg|last=Rosenthal|date=March 8, 2015|access-date=March 8, 2015|archive-date=November 8, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201108200608/https://www.nfl.com/news/brandon-flowers-chargers-agree-to-4-year-36m-deal-0ap3000000477279|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="spotrac"/> He announced that he would switch from No. 26 to No. 24 after it became available following the departure of [[Ryan Mathews (American football)|Ryan Mathews]]. He previously wore No. 24 during his time with the Kansas City Chiefs. He entered training camp slated as the ''de facto'' No. 1 starting cornerback. Head coach Mike McCoy named him and Jason Verrett the starting cornerbacks to begin the season with [[Patrick Robinson (cornerback)|Patrick Robinson]] as the starting nickelback.

He was inactive for the Chargers' 14–31 loss at the [[2015 Minnesota Vikings season|Minnesota Vikings]] in Week 3 due to a knee injury. In Week 4, Flowers set a season-high with seven combined tackles (six solo) and made two pass deflections during a 30–27 victory against the [[2015 Cleveland Browns season|Cleveland Browns]]. In Week 13, Flowers recorded one solo tackle before exiting during the first quarter of the Chargers' 3–17 loss against the [[2015 Denver Broncos season|Denver Broncos]] due to a knee injury.<ref>{{cite web| title=Pro-Football-Reference: Brandon Flowers Game Logs (2015)| url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/F/FlowBr99.htm| access-date=April 21, 2025| website=Pro-Football-Reference.com| archive-date=December 15, 2024| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241215154616/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/F/FlowBr99.htm| url-status=live}}</ref>  On December 12, 2015, the Chargers officially placed him on [[injured reserve]] due to his knee injury and he remained inactive for the last four games (Weeks 14–17) of the season.<ref>{{cite web| title=Chargers Place Brandon Flowers, Corey Liuget on Injured Reserve| url=https://www.boltsfromtheblue.com/2015/12/12/10000976/chargers-place-brandon-flowers-corey-liuget-on-injured-reserve| access-date=April 21, 2025| website=boltsfromtheblue.com| date=December 12, 2015| author=John Lee| archive-date=March 31, 2023| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230331194509/https://www.boltsfromtheblue.com/2015/12/12/10000976/chargers-place-brandon-flowers-corey-liuget-on-injured-reserve| url-status=live}}</ref>  He finished the season with 33 combined tackles (29 solo) and only four pass deflections in 11 games and 10 starts.<ref name="career"/>

====2016====
Throughout training camp, he competed to regain his starting role at cornerback against Jason Verrett and [[Casey Hayward]]. Head coach Mike McCoy named him and Jason Verrett the starting cornerbacks to begin the season.<ref>{{cite web| title=First Look at 2016 Depth Chart| url=https://www.chargers.com/news/first-look-at-2016-depth-chart-134631| access-date=April 21, 2025| website=Chargers.com| date=August 8, 2016| archive-date=April 27, 2025| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250427134255/https://www.chargers.com/news/first-look-at-2016-depth-chart-134631| url-status=live}}</ref>

On September 11, 2016, Flowers started in the [[2016 San Diego Chargers season|San Diego Chargers']] season-opener at the [[2016 Kansas City Chiefs season|Kansas City Chiefs]] and set a season-high with eight solo tackles during a 27–33 overtime loss. On September 25, 2016, he made four combined tackles (three solo) before exiting late in the fourth quarter of a 22–26 loss at the [[2016 Indianapolis Colts season|Indianapolis Colts]] after suffering a concussion in an accidental collision with running back [[Frank Gore]], who was bring tackled by [[Denzel Perryman]]. The blow grounded Flowers on the turf for a few seconds and he would subsequently remain inactive for the next four games (Weeks 4–7).<ref>{{cite web| title=Brandon Flowers, a whirlwind at 30| url=https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2016/11/09/brandon-flowers-a-whirlwind-at-30/| access-date=April 21, 2025| website=sandiegouniontribune.com| date=November 12, 2016}}</ref> In Week 9, Flowers made five solo tackles, set a season-high with three pass deflections, and had a pick-six that marked his last touchdown and interception of his career during a 43–35 victory against the [[2016 Tennessee Titans season|Tennessee Titans]]. He picked off a pass by [[Marcus Mariota]] to wide receiver [[Kendall Wright]] in the fourth quarter and returned it 33–yards for a touchdown to help secure the Chargers' victory. On November 13, 2016, Flowers made three combined tackles (two solo) before being carted off the field in the third quarter of a 24–31 loss against the [[2016 Miami Dolphins season|Miami Dolphins]]. Flowers laid prone on the field after taking an accidental blow to his head when wide receiver [[Jarvis Landry]] delivered a block to his back as Flowers attempted to tackle quarterback [[Ryan Tannehill]] who was scrambling during a 18–yard touchdown pass. The block from Landry knocked Flowers into Tannehill, making his head collide with Tannehill's hip that would snap Flowers head back. Although the play should have been called back, the Dolphins were instead awarded the touchdown and this would be the last time Flowers would appear in a game as he was carted off the field as players knelt in silence.<ref>{{cite web| title=Notebook: Chargers CB Brandon Flowers suffers concussion| url=https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2016/11/14/notebook-chargers-cb-brandon-flowers-suffers-concussion/| access-date=April 21, 2025| website=sandiegouniontribune.com| date=November 14, 2016| author=Michael Gehlken}}</ref> On December 14, 2016, the Chargers officially placed him on injured reserve.<ref>{{cite web|title=Chargers Place Brandon Flowers on IR Among Trio of Moves|url=http://www.chargers.com/news/2016/12/14/chargers-place-brandon-flowers-ir-among-trio-moves|author=Henne, Ricky|website=Chargers.com|date=December 14, 2016}}</ref>

On March 7, 2017, the [[2017 Los Angeles Chargers season|Los Angeles Chargers]] officially released Flowers.<ref>{{cite web|title=Chargers Release Trio of Vets Including CB Brandon Flowers|url=http://www.chargers.com/news/2017/03/07/chargers-release-trio-vets-including-cb-brandon-flowers|author=Henne, Ricky|website=Chargers.com|date=March 7, 2017|access-date=March 7, 2017|archive-date=November 21, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171121214507/http://www.chargers.com/news/2017/03/07/chargers-release-trio-vets-including-cb-brandon-flowers|url-status=live}}</ref>

On August 8, 2017, Flowers announced his retirement from the NFL.<ref>{{cite web|title=Veteran CB Brandon Flowers plans to retire Tuesday|url=http://www.nfl.com/news/story/0ap3000000826976/article/veteran-cb-brandon-flowers-plans-to-retire-tuesday|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170809001254/http://www.nfl.com/news/story/0ap3000000826976/article/veteran-cb-brandon-flowers-plans-to-retire-tuesday|url-status=dead|archive-date=August 9, 2017|website=NFL.com|date=August 7, 2017}}</ref>

'''Brandon Carey Carr''' (born May 19, 1986) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[cornerback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Kansas City Chiefs]], [[Dallas Cowboys]], and [[Baltimore Ravens]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Grand Valley State Lakers football|Grand Valley State Lakers]] and was selected by the Chiefs in the fifth round of the [[2008 NFL draft]]. Carr was the active leader for [[List of most consecutive starts and games played by National Football League players#Active leaders|consecutive starts]] by an NFL defensive player. He also gained notoriety for being the player covering [[Odell Beckham Jr.]] during his famous catch.

==Early life==
Carr was born and raised in [[Flint, Michigan]]. He attended [[Carman Ainsworth High School]]. Carr was a two-way player as a senior, making 53 tackles and two interceptions at cornerback, while having 24 receptions for 431 yards and four [[touchdown]]s at [[wide receiver]].

Carr was named to the All-conference defensive team at the end of the season. He also [[Letterman (sports)|lettered]] in [[basketball]].

==College career==
At [[NCAA Division II|Division II]] Grand Valley State, Carr played in 49 games, [[Starting lineup|starting]] 41. He made 206 [[Tackle (football move)|tackles]] (147 solo) and 11 [[interception]]s, and [[Pass deflected|defended]] 39 passes in his college career.

As a sophomore and junior, Carr helped the Lakers win back-to-back [[NCAA Division II Football Championship]]s. As a senior, he played in all 13 games, posting 45 tackles (33 solo), two interceptions, and defended 13 passes. Carr received the Defensive Back of the Year honor by [[Great Lakes Intercollegiate Athletic Conference]] for his senior season.<ref name=Chiefs1/>

==Professional career==
===Pre-draft===
Carr did not receive an invitation to the [[NFL Scouting Combine]] or to any All-Star games due to his limited exposure attending Grand Valley State. On March 10, 2008, Carr attended Central Michigan's pro day and performed the majority of drills, but opted to skip the bench press. He also attended a pre-draft visit with the [[Kansas City Chiefs]].<ref name="Edwards"/> At the conclusion of the pre-draft process, Carr was projected to be a sixth or seventh-round pick by NFL draft experts and scouts. He was ranked as the 25th best cornerback prospect in the draft by DraftScout.com.<ref name="scout"/>
